title: Can urticaria images found on the internet be a source of health information?
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of the top 100 Google Images results for 'urticaria' (English) and 'urtiker' (Turkish). Two allergy/immunology specialists judged, against clinical criteria, whether each image actually depicted urticaria and/or angioedema; 26.4% of the 178 included images 'had neither urticaria nor angioedema' and the paper concludes 'approximately one-quarter of urticaria images on Google Images did not match true urticarial lesions'. That is a share of items in a sampled corpus judged inaccurate against expert ground truth = CONTENT. Separate blur/resolution/quality ratings are QUALITY.

estimates.country: Not stated for the images; searches were run from Turkey (authors in Adana/Ankara) in English and Turkish
estimates.measure_type: % of retrieved urticaria images that depicted neither urticaria nor angioedema (i.e. did not match the condition searched for)
estimates.value_raw: 26.4% of 178 images had neither urticaria nor angioedema (47/178; 14 of 87 English-term images and 33 of 91 Turkish-term images)
estimates.denominator: 178 photographs retrieved from the first 100 Google Images results for 'urticaria' (87 eligible) and 'urtiker' (91 eligible), after removing duplicates, illustrations, non-photographs and dead links
estimates.definition: Image assessed by two allergy/immunology specialists as showing neither urticaria nor angioedema, despite being returned by a search for urticaria
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition; the paper frames inaccurate depiction as misinformation: 'the potential for misinformation encountered online may influence the diagnosis and course of the disease' and 'approximately one-quarter of urticaria images on Google Images did not match true urticarial lesions'
estimates.source_quote: Results: A total of 178 images were included, with 87 from the “urticaria” search term and 91 from the “ürtiker” search term—71.3% images had isolated urticaria, 1.7% had isolated angioedema, 0.6% had both urticaria and angioedema, and 26.4% had neither urticaria nor angioedema; 131 photographs depicting urticaria and/or angioedema were analyzed.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent researchers specializing in allergy and immunology, both clinically active in urticaria, reviewed all photographs simultaneously and reached consensus on all evaluations; no kappa or independent-double-coding reliability reported
estimates.moderator_quote: On September 14, 2024, the terms “urticaria” and “ürtiker” were searched on Google Images using a private web browser to avoid personalization bias. ... we evaluated the top 100 search results in both languages ... The evaluation of 178 photographs meeting the assessment criteria was conducted by two independent researchers specializing in allergy and immunology ... All photographs were reviewed simultaneously by the two researchers who reached a consensus on all evaluations.
estimates.notes: Primary pooled row; the two language-specific rows below are its components (14/87 + 33/91 = 47/178), so use EITHER this row OR the two language rows, not both. Country coding is a judgement call: the images themselves have no stated country, the search was executed from Turkey, and the English-term corpus is globally accessible content.

estimates.measure_type: % of urticaria/angioedema images rated bad or average quality in the Google Images preview

estimates.definition: Image rated 'bad/average' rather than 'good/very good' on the authors' clarity/resolution/quality assessment of the Google Images preview
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two allergy/immunology specialists rating clarity, resolution and quality by consensus; no reliability statistic
estimates.moderator_quote: Photograph Quality: Photographs were evaluated based on clarity, resolution, and quality, both in the preview section and after the link was opened.
estimates.notes: QUALITY construct (subjective quality rating, no veracity ground truth) - keep out of prevalence pools. After opening the link the same images were 81.7% good/very good, so the quality figure is an artefact of thumbnail rendering. QUOTE NOTE: quote is the contiguous Table 2 block (Quality rows); columns are ‘urticaria’ (n=73), “ürtiker” (n=58), Total (n=131), p-value.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) blur/resolution rows in Table 2 (75.6% blurry in preview, 19.8% after opening; 42.0% poor resolution) - same QUALITY construct as the row kept, redundant; (b) all lesion-morphology, gender, age and body-location distributions in Table 1 - descriptions of the depicted lesions, not veracity; (c) uploader-source distribution in Figure 2 (72.5% of Turkish-term images uploaded by clinics, 47.1% of English-term) - provenance, not a misinformation share; (d) 99.6% of chronic urticaria patients use ICTs / 62.4% of images showed definite urticarial lesions - both cited from other papers (refs 9, 10), barred by R8. Judgement call: whether an image returned for 'urticaria' that shows a different skin condition counts as inaccurate CONTENT or merely off-topic retrieval; I coded CONTENT because the raters are experts applying a clinical ground truth, the paper states the images 'did not match true urticarial lesions', and it frames the finding as online misinformation. breadth='false' (factually incorrect depiction) rather than 'misleading' is arguable. Data-collection date is internally inconsistent (Methods: 14 September 2024; Discussion: 4 September 2024).

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of the first 100 Google Images results for one English and one Turkish search term (14 Sep 2024, private browsing to avoid personalization); 22 items excluded as duplicates/illustrations/non-opening, leaving 178; two allergy-immunology specialists rated every image jointly and by consensus (no independent double coding, no kappa, no formal codebook validation); descriptive statistics only, chi-square/Fisher/McNemar for comparisons; single search engine, single time point, no sensitivity analysis.
rob.item6_quote: Assessment of Urticaria/Angioedema: The presence of urticaria, angioedema, or both in the photograph was recorded; if neither urticaria nor angioedema was present, the condition represented by the lesion was noted.
